title: The Lion's Footprint
paragraphs: A hunter who was both cowardly and boastful set out on the trail of a lion, came to a forest, and asked a woodcutter he met:
— Brother, have you come across a lion around here, or at least its footprint?
The woodcutter said:
— I saw the lion itself; if you wish, come—I will take you to where it is.
The hunter, his face gone pale, replied:
— No, my dear fellow, thank you. I was looking not for the lion itself, but for its footprint.
A man is known not by his claims, but by how he acts in the moment of trial. From afar there are many who "hunt the lion"; face to face, most of them draw back.

title: The Donkey's Law
paragraphs: One day the donkey became king of the forest. A few days later he issued a law: everyone must go to sleep at six in the evening and wake at six in the morning. For twelve hours complete silence must reign in the forest, and whoever broke the law must be punished.
In this fashion, for a time, all sound and stir in the forest ceased.

One day the rooster woke at five in the morning and began to crow. The forest was thrown into uproar. A court was convened at once, and by the donkey's decree the rooster was put to death. From that day on, for fear of the king, no one dared touch the law.
Years passed; the donkey grew old and feeble. He withdrew to a corner of the forest and waited for death. The lion came to inquire after him, then asked:

— You are living your last days now. We wish to know: what was the wisdom of that law which ordered sleep at six in the evening and rising at six in the morning? More than once we wished to rise in revolt and abolish it, yet we held back, fearing the peace of the forest would be broken. We said to ourselves that surely there was some wisdom in this law that we did not understand.
The donkey smiled and answered:
— To tell the truth, I myself have wondered for years: why did the wild beasts of the forest submit like sheep to this law I drew from my own asininity?

The lesson: What keeps a senseless law in force is not the strength of the one who made it, but the silence of those who obey. People often assume that behind an order lies some unseen wisdom, when sometimes behind it stands only the asininity of the one who gave the order. So do not be afraid to ask: an unanswered question turns the most enduring nonsense into law.
What keeps a senseless law in force is not the strength of the one who made it, but the silence of those who obey.

title: The Elephant and the Rope
paragraphs: A traveler passing a place where elephants were kept suddenly stopped: he was greatly astonished to see these enormous animals fastened to a stake by nothing more than a short rope around a front leg. There was neither chain nor cage. Under such conditions it would seem natural that the elephants could break the rope at any moment and escape with ease—yet they did not even appear to try. The man approached a nearby trainer and asked why these magnificent creatures stood obediently in place and had no wish to flee.
The trainer explained thus:

— When the elephants are young, still small, a short rope is enough to hold them. As they grow, they gradually come to believe that they will never be able to break the rope and escape. They think that this rope will still hold them and will not let them go free.
Hearing this, the man was struck with wonder. Imagine: these animals could be free at any moment, yet believing it impossible, they remained tied to the spot where they stood.
What binds us is often not the rope, but the distrust born of past failures. Without breaking the fear of "what will people say," freedom is not possible.

title: Two Donkeys
paragraphs: Two donkeys were going along the road. They saw a monkey sitting in a tree. They said, come—let us tease this monkey: ask him whether he has a friend or not. If he says "I have," we will say "what fool is friends with you?"; if he says "I haven't," we will say "what fool would be friends with you?" They drew near the tree and asked: "Monkey, do you have a friend?" Looking down from above at the donkeys who meant to mock him, the monkey said:
— Wherever I look, all I see are donkeys; with whom should I make friends?
A trap set to humiliate another often springs on the head of the one who set it. He who sets out to mock becomes the joke himself.

title: A Fly in the China Shop
paragraphs: If a fly wished to wreck a china shop, it would not have the strength; but if it got into an ox's ear, that ox, in panic, would smash the shop to pieces.
That fly is nothing but superstition, falsehood, or prejudice. And that ox is the idle, ignorant person himself.
A small lie that enters the ear of the ignorant becomes a great ruin. The way to guard against it is knowledge and moral values.

title: The Hunter's Description
paragraphs: Until the lion learns to write, every story will praise the hunter.
African proverb
Whoever tells the story becomes its hero. If you do not learn to write your own truth, others will always speak for you.

title: The Ant That Carries Water
paragraphs: According to legend, Nimrod (a Biblical figure, ruler of the land of Shinar), seeing the Prophet Abraham as an obstacle to his cruelty, wished to punish him by casting him into the fire. In the middle of the square he had a vast bonfire built. Seeing the fire, every living creature turned to flee.
Just then an ant, with a drop of water in its mouth, began to run anxiously toward the bonfire.
Another ant who saw it asked:
— Where are you running in such a hurry?
— Have you not heard? Nimrod is going to cast the Prophet Abraham into the fire, — said the water-carrying ant, making no secret of its distress.

— Surely you have not seen that bonfire. It is a vast blaze; there is no recourse but to flee. With that one drop of water in your mouth—do you mean to put it out? — the second ant asked with a sneer.
The water-carrying ant replied:
— Even if I cannot put it out, at least it will be clear whose side I was on.
Even if you cannot succeed, at least stand with what is right. When the one you love is in distress, simply being there is a worth of its own.

title: The Turtle's Wrong Calculation
paragraphs: They ask the turtle:
— How long will it take you to reach the village nearby?
— Counting the rain, the mud, the wind, and the ups and downs of the road, it is a three-day journey—but I will get there in six days… — the turtle answers.

Six days later they look and see that the turtle has still not reached the village. They search and at last find it halfway along the road: — Good heavens, you could not cover a three-day road even in six days? — they ask in astonishment.

The turtle answers dejectedly: — Don't even speak of it, friends. I reckoned the rain, the mud, the wind, and the ups and downs—but alas, it never crossed my mind to reckon on wicked people. Whenever I began to move a little faster, they caught me and turned me on my back.
In life every hardship can be calculated—but not people of ill intent. May God set you among those who support you, not those who will not let you go forward.
